questions.text: Which statement best captures the economic problem of scarcity?

options.a: Every good has a positive money price.
options.b: Resources are limited relative to the wants they could be used to satisfy.
options.c: People are unable to compare alternative uses of resources.
options.d: Firms always face shortages of labor.

questions.text: Microeconomics is primarily concerned with

options.a: the determination of a country’s long-run growth rate only.
options.b: the accounting rules used to construct the balance of payments.
options.c: the measurement of national income and aggregate unemployment only.
options.d: the behavior and choices of individual economic decision makers such as consumers and firms.

questions.text: Which of the following can be a microeconomic question?

options.a: What determines the national unemployment rate over the business cycle.
options.b: How a tax on a particular good changes the choices of consumers and firms in that market.
options.c: How aggregate output is measured in national accounts.
options.d: How the overall price level changes across the entire economy.

questions.text: An economic model is best described as

options.a: a simplified formal description of an economic problem built on explicit assumptions.
options.b: a forecast that is valid only if every variable is endogenous.
options.c: a complete description of reality with no simplifying assumptions.
options.d: a historical narrative that contains no variables.

questions.text: In an economic model, an exogenous variable is a variable whose value is

options.a: chosen by the consumer in the objective function.
options.b: taken as given by the model.
options.c: determined by solving the model.
options.d: always equal to zero in equilibrium.

questions.text: In an economic model, an endogenous variable is a variable whose value is

options.a: measured outside the model but not explained by it.
options.b: fixed by assumption and never allowed to change.
options.c: necessarily controlled by the government.
options.d: determined within the model.

questions.text: Constrained optimization refers to

options.a: maximizing every possible objective at the same time.
options.b: comparing two equilibria after an exogenous change.
options.c: choosing the best feasible alternative while respecting restrictions on the choice.
options.d: setting prices so that quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.

questions.text: In a constrained optimization problem, the objective function describes

options.a: the exogenous variables that must remain constant forever.
options.b: the restrictions that define the feasible set.
options.c: the price adjustment rule that clears a market.
options.d: the relationship the decision maker seeks to maximize or minimize.

questions.text: In a constrained optimization problem, a constraint is

options.a: the marginal benefit of the last unit chosen.
options.b: the value of the objective at the optimum.
options.c: a variable determined only after equilibrium is reached.
options.d: a restriction or limit imposed on the decision maker’s choices.

questions.text: The standard rational-choice assumption used in the slides is that a decision maker

options.a: tries to choose the best alternative available to them.
options.b: never changes behavior when incentives change.
options.c: always chooses the cheapest alternative regardless of preferences.
options.d: always has perfect information about every future event.

questions.text: Why can a brewery optimally split an advertising budget between TV and radio even if TV generates more total sales than radio at every equal spending level?

options.a: Radio advertising must have a larger total effect at every spending level.
options.b: Optimal allocation depends on marginal effects, not simply on total effects at equal spending levels.
options.c: Rational firms ignore diminishing marginal effects when allocating a fixed budget.
options.d: The budget constraint does not apply to advertising decisions.

questions.text: The term “marginal” in microeconomics refers to

options.a: the change in a dependent variable caused by a small additional unit of an independent variable.
options.b: a change in an exogenous variable that leaves all endogenous variables fixed.
options.c: the total level of a variable before any choice is made.
options.d: the average value of all feasible alternatives.

questions.text: Diminishing marginal impact of advertising means that

options.a: the first euro spent has no effect on sales.
options.b: the marginal impact is constant at every level of spending.
options.c: total sales must eventually become negative.
options.d: additional spending generates smaller and smaller increments in sales as spending rises.

questions.text: An equilibrium is a state that

options.a: must involve zero profits for every firm in every market.
options.b: can exist only when government fixes the market price.
options.c: will persist as long as relevant exogenous factors remain unchanged.
options.d: requires every individual to consume identical bundles.

questions.text: The equilibrium principle used for the apartment market says that prices adjust until

options.a: quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.
options.b: all apartments have identical quality.
options.c: every renter has the same reservation price.
options.d: the supply curve becomes horizontal.

questions.text: A renter’s reservation price is

options.a: the rent of the renter’s outside option by definition.
options.b: the lowest rent a landlord is legally allowed to charge.
options.c: the highest rent the renter is willing to pay for an apartment.
options.d: the market-clearing rent after all trades occur.

questions.text: All else equal, when the rental price of city-center apartments falls, the quantity demanded tends to

options.a: increase because more potential renters have reservation prices above the rent.
options.b: remain unchanged because reservation prices adjust one-for-one with rent.
options.c: become zero unless the price equals the equilibrium price.
options.d: decrease because supply is fixed in the short run.

questions.text: In the short-run apartment-market example, the supply curve is vertical because

options.a: the number of available apartments is fixed in the short run.
options.b: demand is perfectly elastic.
options.c: the equilibrium price is fixed by assumption.
options.d: landlords have identical reservation prices.

questions.text: If the apartment rent is below the equilibrium rent, then

options.a: quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded and the rent tends to rise.
options.b: quantity demanded is below quantity supplied and the rent tends to fall.
options.c: quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied and the rent tends to rise.
options.d: quantity demanded equals quantity supplied automatically.

questions.text: If the apartment rent is above the equilibrium rent, then

options.a: quantity demanded and quantity supplied both become zero.
options.b: quantity demanded is below quantity supplied and the rent tends to fall.
options.c: quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied and the rent tends to rise.
options.d: the market must remain permanently out of equilibrium.

questions.text: In the simple apartment-market model, an efficient market allocation assigns apartments to

options.a: renters selected randomly, regardless of willingness to pay.
options.b: only those whose reservation price equals zero.
options.c: the people with the lowest reservation prices.
options.d: the people with the greatest willingness to pay.

questions.text: Comparative statics is the method of

options.a: measuring only changes in accounting identities.
options.b: tracing the exact time path by which a market moves between equilibria.
options.c: comparing two static equilibria before and after a change in an exogenous variable.
options.d: maximizing a utility function without any constraints.

questions.text: Comparative statics generally does NOT tell us

options.a: how the equilibrium may differ after an exogenous change.
options.b: which variables are endogenous in a specified model.
options.c: the dynamic path the market follows from the old equilibrium to the new equilibrium.
options.d: whether a supply or demand shift changes equilibrium outcomes.

questions.text: If new city-center apartments are constructed, the standard comparative-statics prediction is

options.a: a lower equilibrium rent with no change in equilibrium quantity.
options.b: an ambiguous quantity effect and a necessarily higher rent.
options.c: a lower equilibrium rent and a higher equilibrium quantity of rented apartments.
options.d: a higher equilibrium rent and a lower equilibrium quantity.

questions.text: Suppose some rental apartments are converted into owner-occupied condominiums, reducing both rental supply and rental demand. Which outcome is unambiguous in the slides?

options.a: The equilibrium rent must fall.
options.b: The equilibrium quantity of rental apartments falls.
options.c: The equilibrium rent must rise.
options.d: The equilibrium quantity of rental apartments rises.

questions.text: When both rental supply and rental demand decrease, the effect on the equilibrium rent can be ambiguous because

options.a: the equilibrium principle no longer applies.
options.b: the supply shift tends to raise rent while the demand shift tends to lower rent.
options.c: both shifts necessarily raise rent by the same amount.
options.d: prices do not respond to simultaneous supply and demand shifts.

questions.text: Which statement correctly distinguishes constrained optimization from equilibrium analysis?

options.a: Constrained optimization studies the best feasible choice of a decision maker, whereas equilibrium analysis studies mutual consistency of choices in a system such as a market.
options.b: Constrained optimization concerns only firms, while equilibrium analysis concerns only consumers.
options.c: Constrained optimization determines exogenous variables, while equilibrium analysis fixes all endogenous variables by assumption.
options.d: They are the same analytical tool with different names.

questions.text: Refer to the accompanying figure. What does the point where the demand curve intersects the vertical supply curve represent?

options.a: A rent below equilibrium at which there is excess supply.
options.b: The maximum reservation price in the market regardless of supply.
options.c: A rent above equilibrium at which there is excess demand.
options.d: The market-clearing rent p* at which the fixed apartment supply equals quantity demanded.

questions.text: If an exogenous variable changes in a model, the purpose of comparative statics is to ask

options.a: which exogenous variable the model should redefine as endogenous after the change.
options.b: how the model’s endogenous equilibrium outcomes change as a result.
options.c: whether the original assumptions can be discarded entirely.
options.d: how to keep every endogenous variable fixed despite the change.

questions.text: Why are assumptions useful in economic models?

options.a: They simplify reality so that important mechanisms and relationships can be analyzed clearly.
options.b: They guarantee that a model will predict every real-world observation exactly.
options.c: They ensure that all economic decisions are unconstrained.
options.d: They eliminate the need to distinguish exogenous from endogenous variables.

questions.text: For prices p1 and p2 and income m, the consumer’s budget set consists of all bundles satisfying

options.b: p1x1 + p2x2 ≤ m.
options.d: p1x1 + p2x2 ≥ m.

questions.text: The budget line consists of bundles that

options.a: cost exactly the consumer’s income m.
options.b: cost strictly less than income m.
options.c: are preferred to every affordable bundle.
options.d: maximize utility for every possible preference ordering.

questions.text: Which statement best distinguishes the budget set from the budget line?

options.a: There is no distinction; the two terms are identical.
options.b: The budget set depends only on preferences, while the budget line depends only on technology.
options.c: The budget set contains all affordable bundles, while the budget line contains bundles that exhaust income.
options.d: The budget line contains all affordable bundles, while the budget set contains only utility-maximizing bundles.

questions.text: If good 2 is treated as a composite good representing spending on everything else, a convenient normalization is

options.d: x2 = 1 for every consumer.

questions.text: With p2 = 1, the budget constraint becomes

options.a: x1 + p1x2 ≤ m.
options.b: p1x1 + x2 ≤ m.
options.d: x1 + x2 ≤ p1m.

questions.text: For the budget line p1x1 + p2x2 = m, the vertical intercept is

options.a: m/p2.
options.b: m/p1.

questions.text: For the budget line p1x1 + p2x2 = m, the horizontal intercept is

options.a: m/p2.
options.d: m/p1.

questions.text: The slope of the budget line when x2 is on the vertical axis is

options.a: m/p2.

questions.text: The absolute value of the budget-line slope, p1/p2, measures

options.a: the opportunity cost of one unit of good 1 in units of good 2.
options.b: the consumer’s marginal utility of income.
options.c: the rate at which the consumer is willing to substitute the goods, regardless of preferences.
options.d: the amount of good 1 obtainable if all income is spent on good 2.

questions.text: Why is the budget-line slope negative when both goods have positive prices?

options.a: Relative prices must be negative for a budget constraint to bind.
options.b: Consuming more of one good while exhausting the budget requires consuming less of the other.
options.c: An increase in income always lowers consumption of both goods.
options.d: Consumers dislike both goods at the margin.

questions.text: If income increases while both prices remain unchanged, the budget line

options.a: rotates around the horizontal intercept.
options.b: shifts outward in a parallel fashion.
options.c: rotates around the vertical intercept.
options.d: becomes steeper without changing either intercept.

questions.text: If income falls while both prices remain unchanged, the budget line

options.a: does not change because relative prices are unchanged.
options.b: becomes flatter but keeps the same intercepts.
options.c: shifts inward in a parallel fashion.
options.d: rotates outward around the x1-intercept.

questions.text: If p1 rises while p2 and income remain fixed, the budget line

options.a: becomes steeper and the x1-intercept moves inward, while the x2-intercept is unchanged.
options.b: becomes flatter and the x2-intercept moves inward.
options.c: shifts outward in parallel.
options.d: keeps the same slope and both intercepts.

questions.text: If p1 falls while p2 and income remain fixed, the budget line

options.a: keeps its slope but raises the x2-intercept.
options.b: shifts inward in parallel.
options.c: becomes steeper and the x1-intercept moves inward.
options.d: becomes flatter and the x1-intercept moves outward.

questions.text: Multiplying both prices by t while holding nominal income fixed is equivalent to

options.a: adding t units of both goods to every affordable bundle.
options.b: dividing only p1 by t.
options.c: multiplying income by t while leaving prices fixed.
options.d: dividing income by t while leaving prices at their original levels.

questions.text: If p1, p2, and m are all multiplied by the same positive factor t, then

options.a: the slope changes but the intercepts do not.
options.b: the budget set expands by a factor t.
options.c: the budget set is unchanged.
options.d: the budget set shrinks by a factor t.

questions.text: Why does perfectly balanced inflation leave the budget set unchanged when income rises in the same proportion as all prices?

options.a: All real purchasing-power ratios and relative prices remain unchanged.
options.b: Every consumer purchases fixed quantities by assumption.
options.c: Nominal income is irrelevant to affordability.
options.d: Inflation necessarily changes the slope but not the intercepts.

questions.text: The numeraire is

options.a: a price normalized to 1 and used as the unit relative to which other prices and income are measured.
options.b: the good with the highest absolute price.
options.c: the consumer’s most preferred good.
options.d: the amount of income left unspent at the optimum.

questions.text: Normalizing p2 to 1 changes

options.a: the budget set unless p1 also equals 1.
options.b: the units in which prices and income are expressed, but not the underlying budget set.
options.c: the physical quantities of goods in every bundle.
options.d: the consumer’s real opportunities and preferences.

questions.text: A per-unit quantity tax t on good 1 changes its effective price from p1 to

options.a: p1/t.
options.c: p1 + t.
options.d: p1 − t.

questions.text: An ad valorem tax at rate τ on good 1 changes its effective price to

options.a: p1/τ.
options.b: p1 + τ regardless of the original price.

questions.text: A per-unit subsidy s on good 1 changes its effective price to

options.a: p1 − s.
options.c: p1 + s.
options.d: p1/s.

questions.text: An ad valorem subsidy at rate σ on good 1 changes its effective price to

options.b: σ/p1.
options.c: p1 − σ regardless of units.

questions.text: A lump-sum tax differs from a tax on good 1 because a lump-sum tax

options.a: necessarily creates a kink in the budget line.
options.b: reduces income without directly changing the relative price p1/p2.
options.c: changes only the slope of the budget line.
options.d: makes good 1 free up to a quota.

questions.text: A rationing constraint x1 ≤ x̄1

options.a: requires the consumer to buy exactly x̄1 units.
options.b: removes otherwise affordable bundles with consumption of good 1 above x̄1.
options.c: increases the horizontal intercept of the original budget line.
options.d: changes the consumer’s preferences against good 1.

questions.text: If good 1 is untaxed up to x̄1 but taxed per unit for consumption above x̄1, the budget line typically

options.a: becomes vertical at every quantity.
options.b: has a kink at x1 = x̄1.
options.c: shifts in parallel without changing slope anywhere.
options.d: remains a single straight line with the original slope.

questions.text: A policy that gives a household a fixed amount of food purchasing power rather than subsidizing every unit of food can

options.a: change preferences rather than constraints.
options.b: be represented only by a proportional increase in all prices.
options.c: never affect the shape of the budget set.
options.d: create a budget set with a kink or flat extension relative to the original cash-only budget.

questions.text: Suppose p1 = €4, p2 = €2, and m = €40. If the consumer buys one additional unit of good 1 while remaining on the budget line, how much good 2 must be forgone?

options.a: 1/2 unit of good 2.
options.b: 8 units of good 2.
options.c: 2 units of good 2.
options.d: 4 units of good 2.

questions.text: Suppose p1 = 5, p2 = 10, and m = 100. The budget line has

options.a: a slope of −1/2, an x1-intercept of 20, and an x2-intercept of 10.
options.b: a slope of 1/2, an x1-intercept of 20, and an x2-intercept of 10.
options.c: a slope of −1/2, an x1-intercept of 10, and an x2-intercept of 20.
options.d: a slope of −2, an x1-intercept of 10, and an x2-intercept of 20.

questions.text: Refer to the accompanying figure. Which change is illustrated?

options.a: An equal proportional increase in both prices and income.
options.b: A decrease in the price of good 2 with income fixed.
options.c: An increase in income with both prices fixed.
options.d: An increase in the price of good 1, holding income and the price of good 2 fixed.

questions.text: Consumer preferences describe

options.a: the technology used to produce the goods.
options.b: how a consumer ranks alternative consumption bundles by desirability.
options.c: the market prices of the goods in each bundle.
options.d: the consumer’s budget constraint only.

questions.text: The notation X ≻ Y means that

options.a: the consumer is indifferent between X and Y.
options.b: the consumer strictly prefers bundle X to bundle Y.
options.c: X contains more of every good than Y by definition.
options.d: X is more expensive than Y.

questions.text: The notation X ∼ Y means that

options.a: the consumer is indifferent between X and Y.
options.b: X and Y have identical market prices.
options.c: X is weakly preferred to Y but Y is not weakly preferred to X.
options.d: X must contain the same physical quantities as Y.

questions.text: The notation X ≽ Y means that

options.a: X costs at least as much as Y.
options.b: the consumer strictly prefers Y to X.
options.c: X and Y must lie on different indifference curves.
options.d: the consumer regards X as at least as good as Y.

questions.text: Preference relations are called ordinal because they

options.a: require every bundle to have a unique market price.
options.b: measure utility in objectively comparable units.
options.c: can compare bundles only when they contain the same amount of one good.
options.d: rank bundles without assigning behavioral meaning to the size of differences between ranks.

questions.text: Completeness of preferences means that

options.a: every bundle is strictly preferred to every other bundle.
options.b: any two bundles can be compared: one is at least as good as the other, or both are.
options.c: every indifference curve is strictly convex.
options.d: all consumers have identical preferences.

questions.text: Transitivity requires that if X ≽ Y and Y ≽ Z, then

options.a: X ≽ Z.
options.b: X ∼ Z necessarily.
options.c: Z ≻ X.
options.d: Y must be strictly preferred to both X and Z.

questions.text: Why are completeness and transitivity useful in consumer theory?

options.a: They guarantee that more is always better.
options.b: They make the preference ranking sufficiently consistent to identify best choices.
options.c: They determine market prices without a budget constraint.
options.d: They imply that all goods are perfect substitutes.

questions.text: The weakly preferred set to a bundle X consists of

options.a: only bundles exactly indifferent to X.
options.b: only bundles strictly worse than X.
options.c: all bundles that the consumer regards as at least as good as X.
options.d: all bundles affordable at the consumer’s current income.

questions.text: An indifference curve through bundle X contains

options.a: all bundles that cost the same as X.
options.b: all bundles strictly preferred to X.
options.c: all bundles that contain the same quantity of good 1 as X.
options.d: all bundles that the consumer regards as equally desirable as X.

questions.text: Why can two indifference curves representing different preference levels not cross under transitive preferences?

options.a: A crossing would imply negative prices.
options.b: A crossing would make both goods discrete.
options.c: A crossing would imply that bundles on supposedly different curves are both indifferent through the intersection, contradicting their different rankings.
options.d: A crossing would violate the budget constraint.

questions.text: Perfect substitutes are goods for which the consumer is willing to substitute one for the other

options.a: only in fixed proportions.
options.b: at a rate that must rise with consumption.
options.c: only when income changes.
options.d: at a constant rate.

questions.text: Indifference curves for perfect substitutes are typically

options.a: vertical lines regardless of which good is neutral.
options.b: parallel straight lines.
options.c: concentric circles around a satiation point.
options.d: L-shaped.

questions.text: Perfect complements are goods that are consumed

options.a: only one at a time.
options.b: at a constant substitution rate.
options.c: together in fixed proportions.
options.d: in quantities determined solely by relative prices.

questions.text: Indifference curves for perfect complements are typically

options.a: closed circles around the origin.
options.b: upward-sloping straight lines.
options.c: parallel straight lines.
options.d: L-shaped.

questions.text: A “bad” is a commodity for which

options.a: the consumer wants the good only in a fixed proportion with another good.
options.b: the consumer is always indifferent to its quantity.
options.c: more of the commodity makes the consumer worse off, other things equal.
options.d: the price is negative by definition.

questions.text: If x1 is a bad and x2 is a good, an indifference curve may slope upward because

options.a: the consumer must be violating transitivity.
options.b: more of the bad must be compensated by more of the good to keep utility unchanged.
options.c: the goods are necessarily perfect complements.
options.d: more of both commodities always makes the consumer worse off.

questions.text: A neutral good is one whose quantity

options.a: must be consumed in a fixed ratio with another good.
options.b: determines the slope of every indifference curve through prices.
options.c: does not affect the consumer’s ranking of bundles over the relevant range.
options.d: always lowers utility.

questions.text: With a satiation point, the consumer has

options.a: an overall best bundle, and moving beyond it in some direction can make a good effectively become a bad.
options.b: no ability to compare bundles.
options.c: monotonic preferences everywhere.
options.d: only straight-line indifference curves.

questions.text: A discrete good is a good that

options.a: has a zero price.
options.b: is always a bad.
options.c: must be a perfect complement to money.
options.d: is available only in integer or otherwise indivisible amounts.

questions.text: For a discrete good, the set of bundles indifferent to a given bundle may appear as

options.a: a set of separate points rather than a smooth continuous curve.
options.b: a continuous circle by necessity.
options.c: the entire consumption set.
options.d: a single vertical budget line.

questions.text: Monotonicity of preferences, as used in the slides, means that

options.a: a bundle with at least as much of every good and more of at least one good is strictly preferred.
options.b: averages are always strictly preferred to extremes.
options.c: all goods are perfect substitutes.
options.d: utility must be cardinal.

questions.text: Under monotonic preferences over two goods, indifference curves are typically downward sloping because

options.a: the budget line is always tangent to the indifference curve.
options.b: both goods are bads.
options.c: if one good increases, some of the other must decrease to keep the consumer indifferent.
options.d: prices must have opposite signs.

questions.text: Convex preferences imply that

options.a: weighted averages of two indifferent bundles are at least as good as the extreme bundles.
options.b: indifference curves must be straight lines.
options.c: more of every good can make the consumer worse off.
options.d: the consumer always prefers an extreme bundle to a balanced bundle.

questions.text: The economic intuition for convex preferences is often summarized as

options.a: a requirement that all goods be complements.
options.b: a preference for consuming only the cheaper good.
options.c: a preference for lower consumption of all goods.
options.d: a preference for balanced mixtures rather than extreme bundles.

questions.text: A set is convex if

options.a: every point in the set lies on a straight line through the origin.
options.b: the line segment connecting any two points in the set lies entirely in the set.
options.c: the set contains no boundary points.
options.d: all points in the set have the same utility.

questions.text: Strict convexity strengthens convexity by requiring that

options.a: all indifference curves are linear.
options.b: a nontrivial weighted average of two distinct indifferent bundles is strictly preferred to the extremes.
options.c: the consumer is indifferent among all weighted averages.
options.d: preferences are no longer complete.

questions.text: Perfect-substitute preferences are generally

options.a: strictly convex but not convex.
options.b: necessarily concave.
options.c: convex but not strictly convex.
options.d: neither complete nor transitive.

questions.text: The marginal rate of substitution (MRS) is

options.a: the slope of an indifference curve at a bundle and the rate at which the consumer is just willing to trade one good for the other.
options.b: the consumer’s total willingness to pay for the entire bundle.
options.c: the difference between the two goods’ market prices.
options.d: the slope of the budget line determined only by prices.

questions.text: For ordinary “goods” with downward-sloping indifference curves, the MRS is usually negative because

options.a: market prices are negative.
options.b: maintaining the same utility requires giving up some of one good to obtain more of the other.
options.c: preferences are incomplete.
options.d: both marginal utilities are negative.

questions.text: If good 2 is a composite good measured in euros, the MRS of good 2 for good 1 can be interpreted as

options.a: the consumer’s marginal willingness to pay in euros for a little more of good 1.
options.b: the consumer’s total income.
options.c: the market price of good 1 regardless of the consumer’s preferences.
options.d: the amount of good 1 the government rations.

questions.text: A diminishing absolute MRS as x1 increases is consistent with convex preferences because

options.a: the goods must be perfect substitutes.
options.b: the indifference curve becomes upward sloping.
options.c: the consumer becomes progressively less willing to give up good 2 for additional units of good 1.
options.d: the consumer becomes more willing to give up good 2 as x1 rises.

questions.text: Refer to the accompanying figure. Why are the two depicted curves called “alleged” indifference curves?

options.a: Their intersection would violate the logic of transitive preference rankings for distinct indifference curves.
options.b: Indifference curves are required to be straight.
options.c: They cross the axes instead of the budget line.
options.d: They are too steep to represent preferences.

questions.text: If X ∼ Y and preferences are convex, which statement must hold for the midpoint M = 0.5X + 0.5Y?

options.a: M is incomparable with X and Y.
options.b: M must be indifferent to X under strict convexity.
options.c: X ≻ M and Y ≻ M.
options.d: M ≽ X and M ≽ Y.

questions.text: A utility function represents preferences when it assigns

options.a: numbers equal to the market cost of each bundle.
options.b: higher numbers to more-preferred bundles and lower numbers to less-preferred bundles.
options.c: cardinal units that are comparable across all consumers.
options.d: the same number to all affordable bundles.

questions.text: The utility concept used in standard consumer theory in these slides is primarily

options.a: technological: utility measures physical productivity.
options.b: cardinal: utility differences have a unique behavioral meaning.
options.c: interpersonal: one consumer’s utility can be compared directly with another’s.
options.d: ordinal: only the ranking of bundles matters.

questions.text: If A ≻ B, a utility representation u must satisfy

options.a: u(A) > u(B).
options.b: u(A) < u(B).
options.c: u(A) = u(B).
options.d: u(A) − u(B) = 1 exactly.

questions.text: Why is a utility representation generally not unique?

options.a: Market prices determine only one possible utility scale.
options.b: Utility must be measured in euros, which can be converted to other currencies.
options.c: Any strictly increasing transformation preserves the ranking of bundles.
options.d: Preferences are assumed to be incomplete.

questions.text: A monotonic transformation f(u) is one that

options.a: reverses all rankings.
options.b: maps every utility level to the same number.
options.c: must be linear with slope exactly one.
options.d: preserves order: if u1 > u2, then f(u1) > f(u2).

questions.text: A differentiable transformation f(u) is strictly increasing where

options.a: df/du = 0 everywhere.
options.b: df/du < 0.
options.c: df/du > 0.
options.d: f(u) = 0 for all u.

questions.text: If v(x1,x2) = f(u(x1,x2)) and f is strictly increasing, then v and u
